newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh Biharis demand return to Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh Biharis demand return to Pakistan.

text.p: Hundreds of Urdu-speaking "Bihari" Moslems awaiting return to Pakistan for more than 25 years demosntrated in Dhaka on Sunday, urging Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to persuade Islamabad to take them home.
"We are living a life worse than many animals do," said Mohammad Nasim Khan, chief of the Stranded Pakistanis General Repatriation Commiteee (SPGRC), who led the demontstration.
"Better kill us than keeping us in inhuman conditions in so-called refugee camps," said Khan, old and frail.

The demonstrators, including woman and children, threatened to kill themselves "unless our dream for going home does not come true," and urged Hasina to persuade her Pakistani counterpart Nawaz Sharif to take them home.
They carried placards showing Hasina and her father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, who led former East Pakistan to emerge as independent Bangladesh through a nine-month war in 1971.
Mujib (as he was called) was killed in a 1975 army coup while holding office as prime minister.

About 380,000 Urdu-speaking Biharis -- so called because they migrated to East Pakistan after partition of the British-ruled subcontinent in 1947 -- were stranded in Bangladesh when Pakistani troops surrendered on December 16, 1971.
Nearly 127,000 Biharis were resettled in Pakistan in the early 1970s but the rest have since been living refugee camps.
In 1992 Islamabad agreed to take back 3,000 Bihari families but only 321 families were repatriated before the process stopped following the removal of then Pakistan prime minister Newaz Sharif.
The number has now swelled to about 400,000 while hopes have dwindled.
The Biharis intensified their home-going campaign following Sharif assumed power again in Pakistan after routing his predecessor Benazir Bhutto in Pakistan's last elections.
"We have kept our hopes alive for so long...and will not let them die as along as we will be alive," Khan said.
A section of Biharis, apparently frustrated by the long delay over repatriation, have already revolted against Khan, and set up a rival faction of the SPGRC, headed by Ezaj Ahmed.
A third group have asked the Dhaka government to grant them Bangladeshi nationality for what they said they "have known this country as our homeland."
"Many of our parents have died on this soil and many of us have been born here. Pakistan is a strange land to us," one Bihari said.
Bangladesh has not yet responded to their plea.
